name: Post-Grunge
about: Post-grunge is what happened when the major labels went looking for the next Nirvana. It took shape in 1994 and 1995 with Bush, Candlebox, Live and Collective Soul, bands that kept grunge's thick guitars, quiet-loud dynamics and baritone growl but sanded off the noise and the ambivalence for radio. Dave Grohl's Foo Fighters gave the sound real songcraft; Everclear and Local H gave it bite; Creed and Matchbox Twenty made it the dominant rock-radio format of the late 1990s. By the 2000s Nickelback, Staind and 3 Doors Down had reduced it to a formula of down-tuned verses and anthemic choruses that critics loathed and tens of millions bought. It remains the default sound of mainstream American rock radio.

artists.name: Foo Fighters
artists.why: the genre's one critically bulletproof band

artists.name: Live
artists.why: earnest, enormous, eight million copies sold

artists.name: Collective Soul
artists.why: melodic Georgia hooks over grunge fuzz

artists.name: Creed
artists.why: the late-1990s arena colossus critics hated

artists.name: Matchbox Twenty
artists.why: took the sound to adult pop radio

artists.name: Silverchair
artists.why: Australian teenagers who outgrew the formula

artists.name: Local H
artists.why: the two-man cult favorite of the scene

albums.title: Sixteen Stone
albums.why: Gavin Rossdale's borrowed Seattle moves and gift for a chorus made the first post-grunge blockbuster, better crafted than its reputation allows.

albums.title: Throwing Copper
albums.why: Ed Kowalczyk's spiritual anguish and the band's slow-build dynamics produced the era's most earnest hit record, with Lightning Crashes its unlikely peak.

albums.title: Candlebox
albums.why: Seattle's first major-label beneficiaries of the grunge boom, more classic rock than their flannel suggested, with Far Behind as the keeper.

albums.title: Foo Fighters
albums.why: Dave Grohl played every instrument on a demo-turned-debut whose pop instincts announced that life after Nirvana could sound joyful.

albums.title: Collective Soul
albums.why: Ed Roland's second album stacked December, The World I Know and Gel into a tighter, hookier record than the demo-quality debut.

albums.title: Sparkle and Fade
albums.why: Art Alexakis turned addiction and bad relationships into tight, fuzzy pop songs, and Santa Monica remains the genre's finest three minutes.

albums.title: Frogstomp
albums.why: Three fifteen-year-olds from Newcastle, Australia, mimicked Pearl Jam convincingly enough to top charts, and Tomorrow still hits hard.

albums.title: Rotting Piñata
albums.why: Detroit's Sponge wrapped glam swagger around grunge guitars, and Plowed and Molly (Sixteen Candles) were among the sharpest singles of the moment.

albums.title: As Good as Dead
albums.why: Scott Lucas's two-man band wrote the smartest, most self-aware post-grunge record, with Bound for the Floor its bitter calling card.

albums.title: The Colour and the Shape
albums.why: Everlong, My Hero and Monkey Wrench made the genre's one true great album, a divorce record with the dynamics and craft of a classic.

albums.title: Yourself or Someone Like You
albums.why: Rob Thomas's songs about ordinary unhappiness sold twelve million copies and pushed post-grunge toward the adult pop it would become.

albums.title: So Much for the Afterglow
albums.why: Brighter and more ambitious than its predecessor, with Father of Mine and Everything to Everyone balancing confession and chart savvy.

albums.title: Clumsy
albums.why: Raine Maida's keening falsetto and Arnold Lanni's layered production gave Canadian post-grunge its defining record.

albums.title: My Own Prison
albums.why: Recorded for six thousand dollars, Scott Stapp's grandiose baritone and Mark Tremonti's riffs made four rock-radio number ones from a debut.

albums.title: Human Clay
albums.why: Eleven times platinum and loathed by critics in roughly equal measure, with Higher and With Arms Wide Open as the genre's peak of earnest bombast.

albums.title: The Better Life
albums.why: Kryptonite made a Mississippi bar band into stars, and the rest of the album defined the plainspoken 2000s formula.

albums.title: Silver Side Up
albums.why: How You Remind Me was the biggest rock song of its decade, and the album around it codified everything post-grunge would be mocked for.

albums.title: Break the Cycle
albums.why: Aaron Lewis's wounded ballad It's Been Awhile carried a dark, heavy record that bridged post-grunge and nu metal to the top of the charts.

albums.title: Come Clean
albums.why: Fred Durst's protégés had the hooks, and Blurry and She Hates Me outlasted most of the era's heavier contenders.

albums.title: Audioslave
albums.why: Chris Cornell fronting three-quarters of Rage Against the Machine produced a heavy, soulful record with Like a Stone its lasting song.

albums.title: Disclaimer
albums.why: The South African trio's American debut delivered Fine Again and the template for a decade of dark, down-tuned radio rock.

albums.title: One-X
albums.why: Written during Adam Gontier's rehab stay, it turned private pain into three rock-radio number ones and a multi-platinum run.

albums.title: The Sound of Madness
albums.why: Brent Smith's big voice and Second Chance's crossover made the album the late-2000s commercial high-water mark for the style.

albums.title: Mister Asylum
albums.why: Johnny Stevens's Brooklyn trio brought swagger and grit back to the format, and Lydia earned the genre a rare recent Grammy nomination.
